Author: @ToadstedCroaks
Content:
Yeah, you can tell this had a lot to do with the craziness that can happen when greed tries to catch up with what other greed is doing at that moment.

Team had hands down some of the cheapest products out there, EVERYONE was promoting it on channels ( for your channels ).
Why would they go from being 40% cheaper than some brands to being 10% more expensive than that same brand?  They saw number go up!

It's a mild consolation for myself that I finally went and upgraded my old AM4 rig to AM5 in September. I was immediately feeling the buyer's remorse with such a large purchase, especially after having accidentally taken my memory off my cart before checkout and only noticing it after it all shipped ( and after I made a joke with a friend about how I'm sure I'll forget something ).

I went back and got it, but was mulling over whether I wanted to stick .. with 2 16gb sticks of ram or 2 32gb sticks.  "Do I really need 64gigs of ram?  I mean, I'll probably have this thing for 6+ years again, and gaming could get more out of hand by then, yadda yadda yadda."   I figured what the heck, it's basically buying in bulk discount pricing at this point, might as well ( again .. that buyer's remorse afterwards ).  The same went with buying a few 4tb m.2 drives.  "Do I reaaaaally need 12 Terabytes of storage?!  I got by with 4 just fine.  But games these days! Holy Moley! But why not just fill up my pci lanes at the start instead of having to take it all apart down the road to do it"

But this last few weeks .... man o man.   Can't believe how narrowly I missed another pc hardware apocalypse, after riding out the GPU one earlier this year.  I could have easily spent an extra $1,000, like it was a 5090 or something.   And I doubt I would have even bothered.  With the prices of stuff now, I would have just put it off again until next year.   

These companies are killing it for the average user, because it doesn't matter to them when the hyper enthusiasts and commercial operations will pay anything and buy it instantly without thinking twice.

Author: @allstarsrobin
Content:
This is why we don’t want components to be manufactured only in specific countries, like Taiwan and South Korea. The United States and Europe need their own security of supply and the capability to produce critical components domestically. In a major crisis, where global supply chains are disrupted or shipping routes become unsafe, it would be extremely difficult to source essential parts from abroad.

China controls a large share of global maritime logistics, so if maritime transport is threatened or restricted, access to semiconductors, electronics, and other high-tech components could be cut off almost instantly. Without domestic production capacity, Western countries would be left vulnerable, unable to maintain their own industries, defence systems, or infrastructure during a prolonged crisis.

This is why diversifying manufacturing locations and rebuilding local production capabilities is not just an economic strategy — it is a matter of national and geopolitical resilience.

Author: @razorsz195
Content: I almost feel like newer audiencies into the PC market have just had their first shock. in a computer magazine i found in a charity shop. Back in 1990 8MB of 70pin EDO RAM (which you had to buy in pairs to create the 32bit address Bus) Costed £400. (4x2MB) on the new 486/Late 386 platform. Thats £50 per MB..not GB..8MB Back then was the 8GB of today. Windows 95 needed 16MB to Run and 32MB to run games. So in 30 years. usage progression has large stayed the same. By 1995, when early 3D accelerators were making their debut. the same kits costed around half as SDRAM was introduced alongside EDO SIMM Memory on boards that were beginning to migrate to the ATX standard (with AT Features). You you would still be into a 32MB (8x4MB) Kit for Double that price. Roughly 7900GRE pricing on memory alone, £800 for 32MB RAM..let that sink in. I considered myself so lucky once computers moved from the SDR to DDR era, as it made memory considerably cheaper.

Author: @ramkumarrealm
Content:
“RAM: WTF?” by Gamers Nexus:

Surge in RAM Prices:
RAM prices (DDR4/DDR5) have skyrocketed over the last several months, with increases up to 180% for some kits. The cost to build or upgrade PCs is now drastically higher — some kits that were $100–$150 are over $300–$400, and higher capacities have jumped by $400–$500.

Main Causes:

AI Data Center Demand: Massive AI server deployments are rapidly eating into supply, driving prices up for everyone, especially desktop and gaming users.

Supply Chain Volatility: Earlier oversupply led manufacturers to cut production; now, demand has caught up, but supply is slow to recover, worsening the shortage.

Supplier Prioritization: Manufacturers are diverting the available supply toward high-margin AI/server memory (e.g., HBM), not consumer kits.

NAND & VRAM Also Affected:
NAND flash (used in SSDs) and GPU VRAM are seeing similar price spikes; SanDisk and Samsung have already announced big increases for 2026.

Cartel & Industry Manipulation:
The RAM industry’s three main suppliers (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) are known for price fixing and cartel-like behavior. Historically, they’ve cut production together to keep prices high and have even faced antitrust cases.

No Relief for Consumers:
PC builders and regular buyers have almost no control; even used RAM is getting pricier. Forecasts indicate that prices will get worse or stay high into 2026 — desktop DDR4/DDR5, SSD flash, and GPU video memory are all caught in the AI boom and manufacturer supply squeeze.

Advice:
There’s little consumers can do except maybe buy used RAM or catch temporary sales — but don’t expect prices to drop anytime soon. Industry analysts stress that the market for computing components is being reshaped by “AI infrastructure expansion” and that server and cloud needs are prioritized over home PCs

Content:
Perfect, and when we made all the things unaffortable for normal people because we build bigger and bigger datacenters, burned down the planet to produce enough electricity, trained on every last though any human ever had, we might get a ChatGPT that can answer if there is a seahorse-emoji. 

We have yet to see really good and great applications for AI at the scale it's being build. Yes it's great for medicine, and it has some niche usecases... but the real widespread benefit to humanity? Is generating AI-Slop for shorts, the most generic and bland AI-"Musicians" or writing sup-par bug ridden code worth it? Money is pumped in as if it is the solution to all problems there ever were. Which will not happen, as AI will always be average. Innovation came from brilliant minds, that are above what the general mass is capable of thinking. At the same time even tho it is called artificial "intelligence", it is not intelligent. I can make intelligent sounding sentences, but so can a good few flat-earthers. Just because it is articulated well, does not mean the meaning is correct or resonable. The more I work with AI professionally, the more I just see the blatant flaws it has. It just is not understanding what it does. It's fumbling trough problems, short-circuits on seemingly unsolvable challenges, or just picks a route that does not make any sense at all, an sticks to that. As a developer, I am not really much more productive with AI-Agents. I tried a lot of them, all boil down to the same few flaws that are there since ChatGPTs initial release. In the end, I am still solving the problems, but now with a strange middleman whose quirks I need to consider, while still needing to consider the quirks of the programming language underneath.

Author: @DankHypatia
Content: I run a small systems integration business, mainly servers and high end workstations that use DDR4 server dimms. I don't know much about the desktop memory market, but the price increases on ECC RDIMM/LRDIMM from around August to now has been shocking. One of the most interesting effects that wasn't mentioned here is that prices on the used market have increased far more than retail prices, probably because numerous operations like mine have realized that RAM is a hot commodity and so every "deal" that is below market gets instantly bought up. I used to regularly get 2133-3200 MHz modules (16-64GB dimms) for around 0.5-1.2$/GB just by looking for deals. Those deals are now far more rare and so you will be paying 2.5-6$/GB market prices, about 400% higher than before. Basically, market memory prices have a normal distribution with long tails on the low an high price side. The tail on the low price side is now gone.

Author: @dominic.h.3363
Content:
Looks like I should be even more grateful to my brother for lending me the money that let me double down (64GB) a while back.

Chrome with 66 tabs: 16.3 GB
A 24B parameter LLM running CPU inference, 7000 tokens deep: 17.59 GB

Let that sink in: You're running something from a category of software that required billions of dollars in research, petabytes of training data, and years of development, except a purpose-built, fine-tuned version with enough parameters to outperform the general-purpose browser-version of ChatGPT in a specific domain... and a Chromium-based browser displaying some text and media is competitive with it in resource consumption. Chromium has completely lost the plot...  (Meanwhile Firefox tab suspension works well enough that if you never close another tab ever again, you could have a 55k tab browser session take no more than 27 GB RAM, because those inactive tabs would be nothing more than bookmarks, for a 833x efficiency difference in resource-usage, but I digress, different topic entirely)

If browsers, UE5 games, etc. weren't pissing away 16-32 GB for nothing, most people wouldn't even need more RAM. Average Jane/Joe sitting at home being mad at data centers almost looks like misplaced anger, because the real problem isn't datacenter demand, but the egregiously wasteful software sitting on their home computer.

I wouldn’t be so quick to call this cartel activity when demand is so volatile, while supply is mostly fixed in the short term. Especially with zero evidence and only conjecture ‘that they could’. Content:
Feels like this all over again, just make an excuse (AI) and bam it’s justified! Or is it?

The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) launched an investigation in 2002 under the Sherman Antitrust Act in response to claims from computer makers like Dell and HP that DRAM prices were being illegally inflated. The investigation uncovered a global cartel that operated from approximately July 1, 1998, to June 15, 2002. 

major manufacturers of Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) chips (commonly known as RAM) were found guilty of a large-scale, international price-fixing conspiracy in the early 2000s and faced substantial fines and legal penalties.

Guilty Pleas and Fines: Five major manufacturers pleaded guilty to their involvement in the conspiracy.
Samsung paid a criminal fine of $300 million.
Hynix Semiconductor (now SK Hynix) was fined $185 million.
Infineon Technologies paid $160 million.
Elpida Memory (a Japanese manufacturer) was fined $84 million.
Immunity: Micron Technology was also part of the cartel but received immunity from criminal prosecution in the U.S. in exchange for blowing the whistle and cooperating with authorities.
Individual Prosecutions: Several executives from the involved companies also faced charges, with some receiving jail time and individual fines.
International Action: European antitrust regulators also fined nine companies a total of over €331 million for the same cartel activities in 2010.
Civil Lawsuits: The companies also faced class-action lawsuits and paid out hundreds of millions of dollars to consumers and computer manufacturers who had overpaid for products containing the price-fixed RAM.

Author: @myne00
Content:
If you're wondering why there's a spot price for ram, it's the same as any market.

There's a relatively inelastic amount of warehouse space, and with each stored unit, the risk of not being able to sell it profitably rises.

Fabs want to run at a steady rate. Eg they want to produce 10k per day. They want to have about 2weeks inventory, but probably have space for 4 weeks. So the spot price represents the deviation from the 2 week target. If it hits 1 week, expect spot prices to rise, if it hits 3, expect it to fall.

This is an example only. The real world has a billion variables that cannot be summed up in a short comment.
